o: Heavenly Father, I thank You for this new day You give me. As I open my eyes this morning, I want to acknowledge that every beat of my heart and every breath of air comes from Your generous hand. Thank You, because Your mercies never come to an end and because Your faithfulness is great every morning. Thank You, because You have not despised the humble beginnings of Your servants throughout history, and You do not despise mine either.

Lord, today I place before You my tasks, my worries and my dreams, even if some of them seem small to me. Teach me not to despise the day of small things. Give me a humble heart so that I seek You first, and a mind attentive to Your Word so that it may direct my steps. If today I feel weak, remind me that Your power is made perfect in weakness and that You delight to use those who trust in You.

Keep me from the haste that takes me away from You, from the pride that makes me think I can do everything alone and from the discouragement that whispers that I am worth nothing. Bless my family, my friends and all who will cross my path today. May my words be kind and my works reflect Your love. I give You this whole day, from the first hour to the last, trusting that You are with me. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: On this day, November 10, 1483, a boy named Martin Luther was born in the town of Eisleben, Germany. His parents, Hans and Margarethe, were hardworking people who earned their living from the copper mines of the region. Nothing in that simple home suggested that the newborn would become known throughout the world.

Shortly after his birth, the family moved to the neighboring town of Mansfeld, where Martin spent his childhood. He grew up in a devout home that attended Mass regularly. With the years, he studied, became a monk and devoted himself to teaching the Scriptures. In studying the Bible, he discovered with astonishment that salvation is a gift of God's grace, received by faith in Jesus Christ, and not something a human being can earn by his own efforts.

This discovery transformed his life. Later he translated the Bible into German so that ordinary people could read it in their own language, and his preaching stirred the Reformation, which awakened a new love for the Word of God throughout Europe. Millions of people have found consolation and hope since then in the truths he rediscovered in Scripture.

What matters in this story is not the man, but the God who chooses whom he wills and who accomplishes great things from small beginnings. A child born into a family of miners, in a town few remembered, was used by the Lord to put the Bible back into the hands of the people. This is how God acts: he looks neither at appearance nor at origin, but at a heart willing to believe his Word.
m: Today's story reminds us that God does not measure the value of a life by its beginning. Martin Luther was born into a family of miners, without riches or fame, and yet God used him to give the Bible back to the people. The psalmist expresses it beautifully: the Lord raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap. God delights in taking what the world considers small to show his glory.

The apostle Paul wrote to the Corinthians that God chose what is foolish, weak and despised in the world, so that no one might boast before him. This is a great consolation. Perhaps today you feel unprepared, with few resources or with a difficult past. But it is not your origin that decides your future; it is God's grace at work in you when you entrust yourself to him with simplicity.

Notice also something else: Luther did not change his time by the strength of his arms, but because he opened the Bible and believed what it said. His strength was in the Word. The same can happen in your life, in your home and in your work, in a simple but real way, when you allow Scripture to guide your decisions and your words.

Practical application for today: before beginning your occupations, slowly read one of the verses of this message and repeat it during the day. Do a small task that others would neglect, with affection, as if you were doing it for the Lord. And when the thought arises that you are not enough, answer it with the truth that God has chosen you and that he will complete the good work he began in you.
m.c: May the God who lifts up the humble sustain you today with his strong hand. Walk with calm, knowing that every step is covered by his care and that nothing awaiting you is greater than his faithfulness. Go out with confidence: he goes before you.

t.s: The Two Blind Men of Jericho
o: Lord Jesus, at the end of this day, I come to You with a grateful heart. Thank You for sustaining me from morning until now, in the easy moments and in the hard ones. Thank You for the food, for the roof that shelters me and for the people You placed on my path today. I acknowledge that I do not deserve so much love, but You give it to me abundantly, and that is why I praise You.

I thank You because You are a God who listens. You hear the cry of the one who suffers, You stop for the one no one takes into account and You answer with mercy. Today I bring You what I do not yet understand, the needs that remain open and the people I love who are going through trials. Open my eyes, Lord, to see Your hand at work even where it seemed to me that You were far away.

Forgive me if, today, I let myself be carried away by worry or if I stayed silent when I should have cried out to You. Take from me fear and anxiety, and give me quiet sleep. May I wake tomorrow with the desire to follow You, like one who has seen Your goodness with his own eyes. I rest in Your arms, trusting that You watch over me all night long. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: Jesus was leaving Jericho on his way to Jerusalem, and a great crowd was following him. By the roadside sat two blind men. They could not see, had no way to make their way through the crowd and perhaps many had long since forgotten them. But when they heard that Jesus was passing by, they did the only thing within their reach: they raised their voices.

They cried out: “Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us!” The crowd rebuked them, telling them to be silent, as the noise of the world so often does to those who suffer. But they, far from giving up, cried out all the more. Their need was too great and the opportunity too precious to remain silent.

Then came the beautiful moment: Jesus stopped. In the middle of the crowd, in the middle of a journey with an immense destination before him, the Lord stopped for two men whom almost no one took into account. He called them and asked: “What do you want me to do for you?” Although he knew what they needed, he wanted to hear it from their lips. They answered simply: “Lord, let our eyes be opened.”

Jesus, moved with compassion, touched the eyes of these men, and at once they received their sight. The account ends with a phrase as brief as it is precious: they followed him. Those who had been healed did not stay by the roadside, but walked with their Healer. The story teaches us that Jesus hears the cry of the needy, that he stops for each one of us and that his mercy gives us light to follow him wholeheartedly.
m: At the end of the day, this story invites us to ask how we pray. The two blind men did not compose an elaborate speech; they simply cried out for mercy. God does not expect perfect words from us, but a sincere heart that acknowledges its need. The psalmist wrote that he loved the Lord because he had heard his voice and his plea, and that as long as he lived he would call on him.

Observe also that the blind men did not let the crowd silence their voice. Perhaps someone told you today that it was not worth insisting, or your own thoughts advised you to be quiet. But Jesus stops for the one who perseveres in crying out to him. Your prayer is not lost in the air; it reaches ears that listen with tenderness, even when the answer is not yet seen.

Notice, moreover, Jesus' question: what do you want me to do for you? The Lord invites you to tell him frankly what is in your heart. You do not need to hide your fears or adorn your requests. Tell him what weighs on you, what you hope for and what you do not understand, then believe that his answer will be good and will come at the right time.

Practical application for tonight: before sleeping, spend a few minutes speaking to Jesus in a low voice and with sincerity. Tell him in one sentence what you need, as the blind men did, and give thanks for three concrete things from this day. Then hand over the worry that weighs on you most and leave it in his hands. If he stopped for two men by the side of a road, he stops for you too.
t.c: Thank you, Lord, for this day lived under your watch. Now give your burdens to Jesus, who hears every cry, and let his peace guard your heart through the night. Sleep quietly and rest without fear: the one who has kept you until now will not go away from you.
